ranges.quote: If a company can email you your password, run. Let me show you what should actually happen when you sign up.
ranges.reason: Second delivery of this line (first attempt at 2.90-6.74 had an odd gap before 'run.'); this take is one continuous confident breath.

ranges.quote: The naive way: store your password in a table as plain text. One database leak and every account is wide open, and people reuse passwords everywhere.
ranges.reason: Single clean take, matches script verbatim.

ranges.quote: So we never store the password. We run it through a one-way hash function, easy to compute forwards, basically impossible to reverse.
ranges.reason: Single clean take, matches script verbatim.

ranges.quote: But hackers precompute rainbow tables of common passwords.
ranges.reason: Clean opening of this beat before the flub.

ranges.quote: So we add a salt, a random string mixed in before hashing unique per user. Now identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed tables are useless.
ranges.reason: Retake of this section (first attempt at 47.28 flubbed 'mixed and hacked' instead of 'mixed in').

ranges.quote: Slow hashes like bcrypt make brute force painful too.
ranges.reason: Clean full retake (first attempt at 65.30-67.18 cut off mid-word).

ranges.quote: Good apps don't store your password. They store a riddle only you can answer. Next episode, we'll talk about how Netflix loads instantly
